blocks.text: I can begin to generalise a sequence.
Given a few numbers, you can carry a sequence on by using a rule. Rules can be shown with diagrams and described in words.
Tap the word to see what it means.

items.def: A sequence is a succession of objects, diagrams or values usually formed according to a rule.

blocks.text: Aisha starts a sequence: 2, 4, … What could come next? Different rules give different sequences.

items: Double each time: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, …
Add 2 each time: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, …
Add 2, then add 3, then add 4, …: 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, …

blocks.text: There is no single answer. Two numbers can be continued in many different ways, and each of them makes a sequence.
Start on −8. Here are three different rules and the sequences they make.
A rule such as “add 10” or “multiply by 10” tells you how to get every next number from the one before.

slides.title: From two numbers to a rule

blocks.text: You are given −2, 10, … Continue it in two ways.
Constant additive: find the difference first. 10 − (−2) = 12, so add 12 each time.
Constant multiplicative: find the multiplier first. 10 ÷ (−2) = −5, so multiply by −5 each time.
Notice that a negative multiplier makes the numbers switch between negative and positive.
Start with 1/10, 2/5, … A common denominator can help. Write 2/5 as 4/10.

items: Multiplicative: 2/5 ÷ 1/10 = 4/10 ÷ 1/10 = 4, so multiply by 4 each time: 1/10, 2/5, 8/5, 32/5, …

blocks.text: You can leave your answers as fractions or decimals. Pick whichever makes most sense.
A sequence starts −6, 12, … Work out the difference or the multiplier, then choose.

blocks.q: Which two numbers come next if the sequence has a constant additive pattern?
Which two numbers come next if the sequence has a constant multiplicative pattern?

blocks.text: Say where the sequence starts AND what the rule is. Then anybody reading your description can write the same sequence.

items: Start on 1 then add 2 each time: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …
Start on 1 then multiply by 3 each time: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81, …
Start on 25 then multiply by 2/5 each time: 25, 10, 4, 1.6, 0.64, …

blocks.text: Lots of different sequences add 2 each time, so it matters to say what you start on.

blocks.q: Choose the description that makes each sequence.

options: Start on 5 then multiply by 0.5 each time
Start on 5 then subtract 2.5 each time
Start on 7 then multiply by 3 each time
Start on 7 then add −3 each time
Start on 9 then multiply by −2 each time
Start on 9 then add −27 each time

blocks.text: A rule can be shown with a diagram. Imagine building towers from rods. Each tower is one value in the sequence: the first tower is the first value, the second tower is the second value, and so on.

items: If one more small rod is added each time, that is a constant additive pattern: the same value is added each time.
If a longer rod is added each time instead, that sequence adds a different value.
Two sequences with the same rule are not the same sequence if they start on a different value.
Two sequences are the same when they are made of the same values in the same order.

blocks.text: Diagrams can help you see how a pattern is developing.
Add two sequences together term by term: first with first, second with second, and so on.

items: P goes up by 3 each time: 2, 5, 8, 11
Q goes down by 2 each time: 10, 8, 6, 4
P + Q: 12, 13, 14, 15. The total goes up by 3 − 2 = 1 each time.

blocks.text: An increase of 3 and a decrease of 2 together make an overall increase of 1 each time.
R goes up by 5 each time. S goes down by 2 each time. R and S are added together term by term.

blocks.q: How does the total change from one term to the next?
blocks.why: +5 and −2 together make 5 − 2 = 3, an increase of 3 each time.

blocks.text: Laura and Andeep make a repeating pattern from counters. One section is: triangle, oval, oval, oval, square. Then the section repeats. Every counter is numbered 1, 2, 3, …

items: Every multiple of 5 is a square: counters 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, …
So counter 25 is a square.
Counters 144, 145 and 146: 145 is a multiple of 5, so it is a square. That makes 144 an oval and 146 a triangle.

blocks.text: Spotting where the pattern repeats helps you work out any counter without drawing them all.
Same pattern: triangle, oval, oval, oval, square, then repeat. Think about the multiples of 5.

items.q: How many squares are there among counters 1 to 200?

items: If we know a rule for a sequence, we can continue it from a starting value.
There can be more than one rule linking two successive numbers in a sequence.
To continue with a constant additive rule, find the difference. For a constant multiplicative rule, find the multiplier.
It is possible to describe a sequence in words if we know enough values: say where it starts and what the rule is.
Rules can be demonstrated with diagrams. This can help us see how a pattern is developing.

flashcards.back: A sequence is a succession of objects, diagrams or values usually formed according to a rule.

flashcards.front: If we know a rule for a sequence, what else do we need to continue it?
flashcards.back:
A starting value.

Start on −8 and add 10: −8, 2, 12, 22, …

flashcards.front: Can two numbers such as 2, 4, … be continued in only one way?
flashcards.back:
No. There can be more than one rule linking two successive numbers.

Double: 2, 4, 8, 16. Add 2: 2, 4, 6, 8.

flashcards.front: What is the rule for the sequence 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, …?
flashcards.back: Add 2, then add 3, then add 4, then add 5, …

flashcards.front: How do you continue −2, 10, … with a constant additive pattern?
flashcards.back:
Find the difference: 10 − (−2) = 12. Then add 12 each time.

−2, 10, 22, 34, 46, …

flashcards.front: How do you continue −2, 10, … with a constant multiplicative pattern?
flashcards.back:
Find the multiplier: 10 ÷ (−2) = −5. Then multiply by −5 each time.

−2, 10, −50, 250, −1250, …

flashcards.front: What happens to the numbers when the multiplier is negative?
flashcards.back: They switch between positive and negative.

flashcards.front: How can a common denominator help with a fraction sequence?
flashcards.back:
It makes the difference or multiplier easier to see.

2/5 = 4/10, so 1/10, 4/10 adds 3/10 each time.

flashcards.front: Why should a description of a sequence say where it starts?
flashcards.back:
Lots of different sequences use the same rule. Saying the start and the rule lets anyone write the same sequence.

Start on 1 then add 2 each time.

flashcards.front: When are two sequences the same sequence?
flashcards.back: When they are made of the same values in the same order (same start and same rule).

flashcards.front: A sequence adds 5 each time and another subtracts 2 each time. Add them term by term: how does the total change?
In a repeating pattern of 5 counters, what can you say about every multiple of 5?
flashcards.back:
They are all the same shape: the last counter of each section.

Triangle, oval, oval, oval, square: counters 5, 10, 15, … are squares.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Securing understanding of sequences
worksheet.instructions: Continue each sequence using the rule named in the question: find the difference (for additive) or the multiplier (for multiplicative) first. Type a minus sign as - and write decimals with a decimal point.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts 1, 3, … and has a constant additive pattern. What is the 5th number?
questions.explanation: The difference is 3 − 1 = 2, so the numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts 1, 3, … and has a constant multiplicative pattern. What is the 5th number?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 3 ÷ 1 = 3, so the numbers are 1, 3, 9, 27, 81.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts 0.1, 1, … and has a constant additive pattern. What is the 5th number?
questions.explanation: The difference is 1 − 0.1 = 0.9, so the numbers are 0.1, 1, 1.9, 2.8, 3.7.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts 0.1, 1, … and has a constant multiplicative pattern. What is the 5th number?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10, so the numbers are 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000.

questions.prompt: A sequence starts −16, 8, … and has a constant additive pattern. What is the 3rd number?
A sequence starts −16, 8, … and has a constant multiplicative pattern. What is the 3rd number?
A sequence starts 25, 10, … and has a constant multiplicative pattern. What is the 4th number? Give a decimal.
A sequence starts −2, 10, … and has a constant multiplicative pattern. What is the 5th number?
In a repeating pattern the section is triangle, oval, oval, oval, square, and counters are numbered from 1. What shape is counter 85?
questions.explanation: 85 is a multiple of 5, so it is the last counter of a section: a square.

questions.prompt: The counter pattern triangle, oval, oval, oval, square repeats and the counters are numbered from 1. How many ovals are there among counters 1 to 200?
questions.explanation: There are 200 ÷ 5 = 40 sections, each with 3 ovals: 40 × 3 = 120.
